Subject: You've read everything. You still haven't moved.

If you've opened every email in this sequence, you probably recognise yourself in the Money Vigilance pattern. You check your balances. You read the articles. You know, broadly, what you should do next.

And you haven't done it.

That's not a character flaw. It's a very specific kind of stuck — the kind where more information genuinely does not help, because information was never the problem.

I work with people at exactly this point. Not to give them another framework to read. To sit with them inside a real conversation about the actual number they keep avoiding, the account they haven't logged into, the decision that's been pending since January.

If that description fits, book a 30-minute call with me below. No prep required. No forms to fill in beforehand. Just a conversation.

Joel
MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner

---
title: "Why do I keep saying I'll sort my finances out next month?"
pubDate: "2026-09-21"
draft: false
---

Most months, Joel's clients can tell you the exact reason this month wasn't the right time. Work was busy. There was a big expense coming. It felt pointless to look at the numbers mid-month when they'd just reset in a few weeks anyway.

The reason changes. The delay doesn't.

Putting it off until next month is not laziness. It is a functional way of managing something that feels, at the level of the body, like a threat. The bank app loads and something in you closes down before you've read a single figure. That response is fast, automatic, and completely outside your conscious control.

What you can influence is what happens in the ten seconds after that feeling arrives.

A client Joel worked with last year described opening her banking app every Sunday evening and immediately switching tabs to something else. She wasn't avoiding the number because she was irresponsible. She was avoiding it because the number had become tangled up with a version of herself she didn't want to confirm.

Untangling that is quiet, specific work. It doesn't require a new system or a better spreadsheet. It requires a honest look at what the number has come to mean.

If you're still reading this, you probably already know which tab you keep switching away from.

The quiz below takes four minutes and tells you something more useful than your credit score.
